idiom_name: schema/IDL artifact + generated or hand-written bindings + per-seam translator and validator
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: define the exchange as a schema artifact (XSD, JSON Schema/OpenAPI, protobuf/Avro/ASN.1 IDL, or an industry standard such as iCalendar) plus the prose that fixes semantics - units, code lists, invariants, examples - and give it a name, a version identifier and an owner. Publish it through a repository every participant can read; generate bindings and validators from it wherever the toolchain allows, and where it does not, hand-write the codec and keep a conformance suite that replays fixtures against the published schema. Each participant translates at its own seam (domain model <-> published language) and validates on ingress, routing invalid payloads to an invalid-message or dead-letter path. Keep the language restrained - only what integration requires - and adopt an additive evolution policy (optional additions, reserved names and numbers, deprecation windows) so participants you cannot see keep working.
pitfalls: Publishing the internal domain model verbatim: consumers couple to implementation details and every refactoring becomes a breaking change for people you cannot see.
No steward and no compatibility policy: the language drifts into per-consumer dialects and 'standard' changes arrive as surprises.
Validating structure but not semantics: schema-conformant payloads still carry wrong units, code lists or invariants unless the prose and the conformance fixtures fix them.

Wrong move: treating an OpenAPI or FHIR schema as proof of runtime behavior -> structurally valid payloads can still violate cross-field or business invariants -> instead combine schema validation with semantic rules, code-list checks and consumer/provider conformance tests.
